# Evaluating the Semantic Specificity of Representation Steering in Language Models

- **Authors**: Zhangdie Yuan, Andreas Vlachos
- **Venue**: cs.CL
- **Published**: 2026-09-01
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.29431>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.29431>
- **Topics**: overthinking
- **Relevance score**: overthinking 0.62

## In one line

Applying a late-layer steering vector to model families where a language model is already competent (Cross-Rule Transfer) reveals that a steering intervention which appears to perfectly fix contradiction blindness is functionally equivalent to a constant logit bias toward the target label, collapsing entailment accuracy from 99.6% to 40.4% rather than repairing a reasoning circuit.

## Problem

Localized Representation Steering is widely used as a causal remedy for reasoning pathologies in LLMs, and standard locality audits (checking for side effects on unrelated tasks) can make a steering vector look like it has repaired a reasoning circuit when it has really just learned to inject the correct output label, because unrelated tasks never elicit the target label and so cannot expose a global label bias. It is open how to distinguish a genuine internal repair from a superficial label override when the evaluation only ever measures accuracy on the target failure mode.

## Contributions

- Proposes Cross-Rule Transfer (CRT): apply a steering vector, learned to fix a target failure, to structurally distinct rule families where the unsteered model already has native competence (>=95% baseline), and check whether that competence collapses.
- Shows late-layer LRS that appears to fully repair contradiction blindness in Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (restoring benchmark accuracy to 100% with apparent zero side effects under oracle gating) collapses native entailment accuracy from 99.6% to 40.4% when applied unconditionally to competent rule families.
- Demonstrates the steering vector is functionally equivalent to a constant scalar logit bias (Direct Logit Biasing, beta=+-3.0): gated DLB matches gated LRS accuracy exactly (1.0000) on the source task, and both give identical accuracy profiles under greedy decoding on downstream tasks.
- Provides four additional controls (shuffle-label control, cross-model grafting Llama->Qwen at 96.6% transfer, early-layer steering control, MLP non-linear probe) all converging on the same conclusion: the vector encodes a label-preference direction, not a repaired reasoning circuit.
- Publishes Asymmetricity-2.0, a >72M-entry procedurally generated NLI benchmark (Wikidata-derived symmetric/antisymmetric/irreflexive relations) used to elicit and measure contradiction blindness across 18 model variants.

## Method

The authors first identify contradiction blindness: instruction-tuned LLMs (evaluated with structured chain-of-thought JSON prompting on Asymmetricity-2.0) predict forward entailment near-perfectly but almost never predict contradiction, across 18 models from 0.5B-9B parameters. They train linear (and MLP) probes on intermediate activations to localize where this failure lives, finding late-layer probes systematically misclassify failing contradiction cases as entailment (error >50% chance), indicating representational compression/collapse toward the output label axis in late layers. They then construct a Localized Representation Steering (LRS) vector per model as the difference-in-means between activations at successful vs. failing instances at a late target layer (e.g. Llama layer 13/16, Qwen layer 32/40), normalize and inject it (scaled by alpha=1.5) into the residual stream at final prediction tokens. Under oracle gating (injecting the vector only on contradiction-rule inputs) this recovers 100% target accuracy with apparently zero side effects on unrelated (entailment) rule families evaluated on the same benchmark. To test whether this is a genuine circuit repair, the authors introduce Cross-Rule Transfer (CRT): they instead apply the same vector unconditionally to structurally disjoint rule families sharing the same output label space where the model is already highly competent (>=95% baseline, e.g. swap_symmetry, transitivity_chain), and check whether that native competence survives. They corroborate the CRT diagnosis with four controls: (1) a Direct Logit Biasing (DLB) baseline that adds a constant scalar bias directly to target-label logits, tuned to match LRS's empirical logit shift; (2) a shuffle control that builds a 'steering vector' from randomized success/failure labels; (3) cross-model grafting of Llama's vector onto Qwen via a learned linear projection between hidden-state dimensions; (4) an early-layer steering control (layer 2 vs. layer 13).

## Results

On the Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct anchor, unsteered baseline is near-perfect on forward-entailment rule families (swap_symmetry 99.67%, transitivity_chain 100%) and complete zero-recall failure on contradiction-detection rule families (symmetric_nonreflexive 0%, symmetric_not_transitive 0%) at 65,536-instance scale; this pathology holds across 18 evaluated models (0.5B-9B params, Llama/Gemma/Qwen/DeepSeek families), with 7/18 showing complete failure and only 2/18 achieving recall>=0.5. Under oracle gating (steering vector injected only on contradiction-labeled inputs), LRS recovers 100% target-task accuracy with zero measured side effects on the competent entailment splits -- but this 'zero side effects' result is an artifact of the oracle gate, which requires a task classifier unavailable at real deployment. Applying the same vector unconditionally (Cross-Rule Transfer) to the entailment rules the model already handles at 99.6% baseline collapses accuracy to 40.4%, injecting 298 false contradiction predictions out of 500 entailment items (McNemar chi^2 in [290.1, 299.8], p<1e-12 across 5 resamples; post-steering accuracy stable at 40.4%+-0.8%). A steering-strength sweep shows no alpha value restores contradiction recall without destroying entailment competence: at alpha<=1.0 steering is too weak to fix the target task at all, and by alpha=1.5 the same collapse occurs. Gated Direct Logit Biasing (a constant scalar bias of beta=+-3.0 added directly to target-label logits, with no learned direction) exactly matches gated LRS's 1.0000 source accuracy and gives identical accuracy on three downstream tasks (CLUTRR, SpartQA, ProntoQA) under greedy decoding, and this equivalence holds under sampling too (temperature 0.7, nucleus p=0.9, kappa>=0.94). A shuffle control (vector built from randomized success/failure labels) still achieves a nominal 100% 'recovery' by simply flipping all predictions to contradiction, because success/failure is almost perfectly confounded with the entailment/contradiction label in the baseline model. Cross-model grafting of Llama's vector onto Qwen-3.5-9B-Instruct (via a learned linear projection between hidden dimensions) transfers with 96.6% accuracy and only 17 side effects, indicating shared late-layer label geometry across architectures rather than a shared reasoning circuit. Early-layer steering (layer 2 instead of layer 13) gives only a modest +15.4% improvement on the target task but 3,465 side effects, showing the effect is specific to late, near-output layers. Token-position ablations show injecting the vector only at the final label token reproduces the full 100% target recovery, while injecting it only during the preceding chain-of-thought tokens gives 0% recovery -- the intervention overrides the output token commitment rather than the internal reasoning trajectory. Auditing on a naturalistic MNLI subset (where the model is natively competent, >=95% baseline) shows the same late-layer steering vector degrades competent accuracy to 35.4%, indicating the failure mode is not an artifact of the synthetic Asymmetricity-2.0 templates. A separate anomaly: for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen3-8B, the same steering procedure yields 94-100% nominal accuracy, but per-instance inspection shows this is a formatting-compliance bypass (the vector forces JSON-label-compliant output) rather than any reasoning repair. All headline numbers come from generative, chain-of-thought inference over the synthetic Asymmetricity-2.0 benchmark and its downstream transfer tasks (no physical hardware distinction is made; there is no separate simulation-vs-hardware split in this paper).

## Limitations

Stated by the authors: (1) Asymmetricity-2.0 is built from Wikidata, which carries geographic/cultural/historical biases and gaps the authors cannot control; (2) the study is English-only, so culture- or language-specific reasoning artifacts in the templates or in English-pretrained models cannot be ruled out; (3) the downstream benchmarks (CLUTRR, SpartQA, ProntoQA) are stylized, structured reasoning tasks and do not capture open-ended conversational reasoning or free-form dialogue where label-token boundaries are less well defined; (4) parameter-level mechanistic validation (e.g. cosine similarity of the steering vector with the unembedding label-direction difference, layerwise logit-lens attribution) is not performed on closed/API-only models and is left as future work -- CRT is explicitly a behavioral, not a weight-level, audit. Additional caveats the reader should note: the steering-strength sweep (Table 7) shows the collapse is threshold-dependent -- at alpha<=1.0 the intervention is too weak to fix contradiction recall at all, and there is no intermediate alpha at which contradiction recall is restored without also destroying entailment competence, so the failure mode is not an artifact of picking alpha=1.5 specifically. Qwen-3.5-9B-Instruct is included only as a directional sanity check, not a valid CRT subject, because its own native competence on the entailment rules (45.2%) falls below the paper's own >=95% competence threshold. The 'zero side effects' headline for LRS holds only under oracle task-level gating (injecting the vector exclusively on contradiction-labeled inputs, which requires a task classifier that does not exist at deployment); under the realistic unconditional/ungated setting the same vector produces the catastrophic collapse. Token-position ablations show the vector's effect is entirely at the final label-decision token (final-token-only injection gives 100% of the effect; injecting only during the preceding chain-of-thought tokens gives 0% effect), meaning the intervention overrides the output commitment rather than altering the internal reasoning trajectory.

## Why it matters here

- **overthinking**: This paper is not about reasoning length directly, but it undercuts the evidentiary basis of any steering-for-reasoning-length method that reports only a benchmark-level accuracy or token-count recovery as proof the intervention 'fixed' the underlying behavior. The paper shows a difference-in-means steering vector, extracted exactly the way length/overthinking steering vectors are typically built, can achieve a clean apparent fix (100% target recovery, zero side effects under gating) while being nothing more than a late-layer logit bias toward one output mode -- and that this bias catastrophically destabilizes performance the moment it is applied outside the narrow condition it was tuned on (unconditional application on competent rules: 99.6%->40.4%). Applied to overthinking work, this is a direct methodological warning: a steering vector that shortens (or lengthens) reasoning chains on the target benchmark should be audited by injecting it on problems/rule-types the model already solves at native length/accuracy, not just reported for its effect on the target distribution -- otherwise a vector that has simply learned to bias toward 'short output' or 'stop token' can look like a semantic fix for overthinking while actually degrading unrelated competence, which is the same shape of failure already suggested by the +454% length blowup from suppressing a 'thinking' feature and by Manifold Steering's backfire-at-high-strength result. It qualifies rather than undercuts steering-based length control outright: the paper explicitly notes its diagnostic (CRT) is construction-agnostic and applies to any steering vector, so it is offered as a validation checklist (Table 10) rather than a blanket rejection of the approach.

## Abstract

Localized Representation Steering (LRS) is widely used to correct reasoning pathologies in large language models. However, standard benchmark evaluations can easily be fooled by superficial label overrides, creating a false impression of reasoning circuit repairs. In this work, we propose Cross-Rule Transfer (CRT), a diagnostic framework that audits representational interventions by evaluating them on rule families where the model is natively competent. Evaluating late-layer LRS for a widespread logical failure, contradiction blindness, reveals that the intervention merely injects a global label bias: applying the steering vector to rules the model already handles correctly (99.6% baseline) degrades performance to 40.4% by forcing false contradiction predictions. We support this diagnosis with four complementary controls (direct logit bias equivalence, control vector label-flipping, cross-model grafting, and early-layer steering checks), providing a rigorous methodology to distinguish genuine reasoning repairs from superficial label overrides.
